headline: Upstream space infrastructure — launches, satellite manufacturing, components and sensors — seen as the key enabler and disproportionate beneficiary of government/defense spending.
reasoning: Vig frames the space economy as upstream versus downstream, with upstream — encompassing launches, satellite manufacturing, components, payloads and sensors — set to benefit disproportionately from government and defense spending. The sector needs significantly more launches, more satellite volume and faster replenishment cycles, but this must be offset by lower unit costs, greater reusability and more vertical integration. Downstream will grow through software, connectivity and analytics serving wider commercial applications.
quote: If you think about the upstream versus downstream debate, upstream I think what you need to see there is very simply more launches. We need significantly more launches than we've had over the last 10 years... we clearly need to see more and more satellite volume. We need to see faster replenishment. I think the more launches we see, the more satellites we see, the more we're gonna need in terms of replenishment, replacements, about aftermarket element is gonna come through. But what I think offsets that is the industry needs to see lower unit costs. There's gonna be more reusability. There's gonna need to be more efficiencies in manufacturing and I think more vertical integration.

reasoning: Vig identifies three principal risks in the space investment universe: first, many new entrants are only three to five years old and have not yet proven they can deliver at scale relative to established defense primes; second, capital requirements are enormous with limited free cash flow and earnings, making valuation difficult to anchor — stocks look expensive on headline multiples; third, national security restrictions on technology transfer may limit cross-border commercialisation and create risk of technology theft.
quote: Number one is we have a lot of new entrants that have yet to prove that they can operate at scale... For a lot of the companies that are in the space now, that's not the case. They are three years old, five years old, some less than that. And so they need to prove that they can deliver on what they've promised and do it at scale. I'd say the second thing is that the investment needs right now are huge. So from a kind of financial perspective, there isn't a great deal of free cash flow being generated by a number of these companies and obviously earnings as well. headline: Europe's $1.8 trillion defense underspend since 1991 signals a multi-decade catch-up cycle in defense and space spending.
reasoning: Vig cites IFO Institute analysis estimating that European countries extracted a 'peace dividend' of approximately $1.8 trillion since 1991, representing the gap between actual defense spending and what would have been required to meet the 2% NATO target. With pressure now mounting to reach 3% (and President Trump advocating 5%), the scale of structural underspend implies a very long runway of defense capex growth. He views demand risk as minimal for the next decade as a result.
quote: The IFO Institute, they did some analysis suggesting that European countries had extracted a peace dividend of about $1.8 trillion since 1991. So what that's effectively saying is, that's the difference between what they should have been spending on defense versus what they actually spent if they'd met the 2% NATO target. Now, where we are today, there's a push to get towards 3%, and obviously President Trump has talked about 5% being the right number given that heightened threat environment. But even if we go to three, that gives you a sense of just how much under spend there's been.

If you'd asked a number of countries 12 months ago, do you think you have sufficient defense to protect yourself against, be it drones, be it missiles, et cetera, the answer from most countries that have been affirmed, yes, absolutely we have. I think now 12 months forward, the answer is a firm, no, we don't. So I think anything to do with that area, I think is severely underestimate in terms of the need to spend. headline: Kraus defends the structural integrity of non-traded BDCs and their 5% redemption limits, arguing that these products have thus far done what they promised despite heightened redemption pressure

headline: Berger highlights multi-strategy market-neutral hedge funds as preferred diversifier vehicle for institutional allocators

He notes that multi-strat engineers embed rigorous risk management to ensure these funds remain uncorrelated during equity selloffs and market stress. The alpha generated provides a return cushion even when the primary value is the diversification, not the absolute return.
quote: People are looking to market neutral hedge funds that oftentimes multi-strat because they're looking for hedge fund portfolios that combine a range of different inputs. headline: Wellington's Berger warns inflation-driven bear markets break the traditional stock-bond diversification relationship, requiring new portfolio tools

In an environment where markets fall because inflation is rising, bonds provide little protection.
